# en-informal

## Good example

Forty boxes and one wet Tuesday

So the basement flooded. Only about an inch, but that was enough to soak the bottom row of the archive shelves, which is where somebody in 2011 decided to keep the old contract files. Forty boxes. I know because I carried every one of them up the stairs, since the lift picked that morning to break too.

Half of them were fine. The other half smelled like a pond.

I spent the rest of the week with Tomasz Example from Facilities, peeling damp Purchase Orders apart and laying them out on the training room floor. We ran out of floor by Wednesday and moved on to the corridor. People stepped over us with their coffee and said things like "wow" and "good luck." Nobody offered to help, and I can't say I blame them.

Here's the thing I didn't see coming. About a third of what we dried out had already been scanned years ago. Nobody knew. There's a spreadsheet, last touched in 2019, sitting in a folder called "misc," and it lists every box by number. Tomasz found it Friday at about 4 p.m. I had to go for a walk.

### Before

In today's fast-paced world of office supplies, I wanted to share my first experience with the new online purchasing catalog, since a few of you asked about it.

I needed to order 10 chairs for the meeting room, so I decided to give it a try. Honestly, it was a lot easier than I expected, and the experience was truly seamless. I found what I needed, placed the order, and the whole thing took about 2 days from start to finish. Not bad at all for a first go.

The only hiccup was that one of the chairs arrived broken. A bit annoying, but I made a report of it through the catalog. Moreover, the vendor's already replaced it. Furthermore, the new chair showed up without any fuss, so I was pretty happy with how that was handled.

Overall, my verdict is positive. It isn't just a catalog, it's a whole new way of ordering. There's a bit of a learning curve if you haven't used it before, but once you get the hang of it, it seems to work well. If you're planning to order anything soon, it's worth a look.

Feel free to message me if you want a quick walkthrough. Happy ordering, everyone!

## Pair 2

### Before

In today's fast-paced world, when I started as a procurement officer, I had no idea how much of my job would involve writing Statements of Work. I thought it'd be a quick task: describe what we need, add a few requirements, and send it off. I was wrong about that, and I learned it the hard way.

Over the past year I wrote 14 Statements of Work. The first one had to be redone twice. The first draft was too vague, so vendors kept asking questions that should've been answered in the document. The second draft swung the other way and had so much detail that it limited who could realistically bid. Only on the third try did I get the balance right.

What helped most? Talking to the people who'd actually use the service. Once I asked them what success looked like, the requirements got truly much clearer. Moreover, I also started keeping a short checklist: the purpose, the scope, the deliverables, the timeline, the measures of acceptance, and the things that are explicitly out of scope.

[cut]

### After

When I started as a procurement officer, I had no idea how much of my job would involve writing Statements of Work. I thought it'd be a quick task: describe what we need, add a few requirements, and send it off. I was wrong about that, and I learned it the hard way.

Over the past year I wrote 14 Statements of Work. The first one had to be redone twice. The first draft was too vague, so vendors kept asking questions that should've been answered in the document. The second draft swung the other way and had so much detail that it limited who could realistically bid. Only on the third try did I get the balance right.

What helped most was talking to the people who'd actually use the service. Once I asked them what success looked like, the requirements got much clearer. I started keeping a short checklist: the purpose, the scope, the deliverables, the timeline, the measures of acceptance, and the things that are explicitly out of scope.

I also learned to read old Statements of Work from colleagues, not to copy them, but to see how others organized their thinking. Some were excellent, some were confusing, and both kinds taught me something.

[cut]
